content:
I’m sorry — that is a horrible thing to be carrying.

If I were in your position, and I was reasonably sure I saw what I saw, **I would tell Lena**. Not to hurt her, not to be the one who “drops the truth,” but because I think she deserves to know before the baby arrives. I would not wait until after the birth, because that would let the next huge chapter of her life start under a cloud. And I would not stay silent forever, because silence can become its own kind of betrayal.

But I would not tell it like a verdict.

I would not say, “Your husband is cheating on you.” I would say something like:

> “Lena, I need to tell you something and I really hate doing this. At the station I saw [husband’s name] kissing a woman. I’m not asking you to decide anything tonight, and I’m not telling you what it means. I only know what I saw. I thought you deserved to know, and I didn’t want you walking through your pregnancy and the next stage without that information. I’m here.”

Then I would stop talking and let her respond. She might be stunned, angry, dismissive, crying, or tell you I’m wrong. If she says she doesn’t believe it, I would not pile on. I would say:

> “I’m sorry. I only told you because I care about you. If I’m wrong, I’m sorry. If I’m right, I’m here.”

I would also not make it public. No telling the husband, no telling mutual friends, no telling family unless she asks or you are genuinely worried about her safety. And I would not turn into a private investigator: no following them, no taking photos, no “checking” further. That crosses a line and can make things much worse.

If there is even a real possibility that you misread the moment — a goodbye, a colleague, an ex, a family member — I would still tell her, but I would leave room:

> “It looked like a kiss. I don’t know what it was. I’m not sure how to read it.”

That gives her the information without you becoming a prosecutor.

The kindest version of this is not silence, and not a bomb. It is: **“I care about you enough to tell you what I saw, and I care about you enough to give you space with it.”**

A baby changes everything. It will not make this easier after the fact; it will make it more tangled, more urgent, and harder to talk about. But she doesn’t need your conclusion. She needs the truth, gently, and your loyalty.
